title: TA9-22285
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXXX XXXXX and XXXXX XXXXX, are citizens of Syria who seek refugee protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 Allegations

The complete story alleging the basis of the claimants' fears is captured in the Personal Information Forms (PIF).2 The claimants allege that due to their interests and attending underground Jehovah's Witness meetings towards the beginning of 2009, that their lives are at risk, particularly in XXXXX 2009 when the male claimant was questioned by the police for three hours, and prior to being released, the male claimant was told if he is caught at Jehovah's Witness meetings that the consequences will be bad. The claimants fear both their relatives and the authorities for their involvement with the Jehovah's Witnesses. The claimants then made arrangements to leave for Canada without their children on XXXXX XXXXX, 2009. Decision

I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. I also find that should the claimants return to Syria they would not be subjected personally to a risk to their lives or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Further, on substantial grounds there is no danger of torture. In determining this claim, the Panel followed the Chairperson's Guidelines3 on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender Related Persecution. Identity
On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimants are citizens of Syria based on copies of their respective Syrian passports as seen in exhibit R/A-2. Analysis

The determinative issues in these case are the credibility of the evidence as submitted and the identity of the claimants as Jehovah's Witnesses. On the issue of credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal case in Sellan4 which stated the following: Where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim. The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

Furthermore, the Federal Court notes the following: The Board is in a much better position than a reviewing court to gage the credibility and plausibility of a refugee claimant's story. A credibility finding is not a finding of mixed fact and law. It is a finding of fact, pure and simple. Findings of fact made by the Board may only be interfered with by a reviewing court if the finding was made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it (see the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)). Indeed, it was Parliament's express intention that administrative fact finding would command this high degree of deference (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] S.C.J. No. 12 (QL) at paragraph 46). Thus, credibility findings of the Board are to be reviewed against the statutory standard of review provided for in paragraph 18.1(4)(d) of the Federal Courts Act (see Diabo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1772, [2004] F.C.J. No. 2168 (QL) at paragraph 3).

It should be noted that the male claimant gave the majority of evidence pertaining to these claims with some evidence given by the female claimant. The male claimant stated that he and the female claimant left Syria due to an incident that happened to the male claimant as it relates to his and the female claimant's meetings with people affiliated with Jehovah's Witnesses. The claimants alleged to being Jehovah's Witnesses and that they cannot practice their new faith as it is banned in Syria.

The claimants are Catholic and Syrian Orthodox respectively by birth and became interested in the Jehovah's Witness faith, as they were more involved in Bible study more than the Catholics in Syria. As Catholics and Orthodox Christians the claimants never had problems worshipping in Syria. The claimants were asked when they realized that their lives were at risk. The claimants responded on XXXXX, 2009 when police suddenly attended their home with a warrant. The male claimant went as required and was questioned about his Jehovah's Witness meetings and released on condition that if he is caught with Jehovah's Witnesses he will be imprisoned.

The panel notes that the claimants have two children, a son born in 1990 and daughter born in 1994. At the time the claimants became interested in the Jehovah's Witness faith, their children were 15 and 19 years respectively. The claimants were asked if the children were taken to Jehovah's Witness meeting while in Syria. The male claimant responded by saying "Of course not as I did not think I could convince them. I brought them up to have their own minds." While it is admirable that the claimants raised their children to have their own minds, it is not credible that the claimants would not have seen it fit to take their children to Jehovah's Witness meetings, towards the beginning of the year in 2009, given their interests in the faith and that Jehovah's Witnesses are involved in Bible study more so than the Catholic faith.

Further, the panel asked the claimants whether there was a time their children learned they were interested in the Jehovah's Witness faith. The response was that the children felt something but they weren't sure as "we stopped going to orthodox church in XXXXX, Syria towards the end of XXXXX 2009." Given the ages of the children at the time the claimants were allegedly attending underground Jehovah's Witness meetings, unless the claimants withheld such information from their children, it is likely that the children would have inquired with their parents, the claimants, as to why they are attending a different faith, given that the children "felt something but weren't sure." The claimants' credibility is negatively impacted in this regard.

In evaluating these cases, the panel has concerns as to the claimants' identity as Jehovah's Witnesses, which allegedly caused their problems requiring them to leave Syria. Their lack of identity as Jehovah's Witnesses would also impact on the credibility of the claims as so submitted. Consequently, it should be noted that the Board, with the agreement of the claimants, sought some evidence as to the claimants' association, membership with the Jehovah's Witness faith while in Canada since October 30, 2009. Exhibit R/A-4 is a letter from Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Canada, dated XXXXX, 2011 stating that the male claimant is not a baptized member of the congregation in XXXXX, but rather he attended Bible study meetings three months prior to the letter being written.

The panel asked the claimants whether in Canada they are baptized as Jehovah's Witnesses. The male claimant responded "right now I am studying and giving sermons on the Holy Bible." The panel then asked given their interests in the Jehovah's Witness in Syria before coming to Canada and the two years since being in Canada, why they are not baptized as Jehovah's Witnesses. The male claimant stated that he considers baptism as important and that the elders will decide if he is ready or not. It was also stated at a later point in the male claimant's testimony, when questioned by his counsel, that he believes he will be baptized approximately in XXXXX 2012 into the Jehovah's Witness faith. If and only if the claimants have been involved with the Jehovah's Witnesses shortly after arriving in Canada, which the panel has no proof of such involvement, there was no credible reason given why credible and trustworthy evidence from parishioners involved in Bible study with the claimants could not have been produced given Jehovah's Witness superiors do not provide such letters to persons. The panel makes a negative credibility finding.

While it is acknowledged that people do decide at their leisure when they will fully commit to a different faith, the panel does not find it credible that the claimants would not have been more involved in the Jehovah's Witness faith, in Canada and commit to the faith by way of baptism given the two years in the country which is significant. Frankly speaking, the panel has little credible evidence that the claimants are involved, as they say they are, in the Jehovah's Witness faith, in Canada, a country that respects religious freedoms.

The claimants provided copies of some photographs as so seen in exhibit C-4, which by no means would satisfy an informed and ordinarily prudent person as to the identifies of the claimants as Jehovah's Witnesses as alleged. It is not unreasonable, in the panel's view, for the claimants to provide satisfactory evidence as to their identifies as Jehovah's Witnesses, and given that their identities as such are in question, the panel is not in a position to satisfy itself, based on the evidence, that the claimants are Jehovah's Witnesses now and had problems prior to leaving Syria which if required to return would put their lives at risk. The panel makes a negative credibility finding.

It should also be noted that the male claimant did provide evidence that contradicts or confuses his earlier evidence as to why the claimants to date are not baptized as Jehovah's Witnesses, which would suggest that they would continue their practices and ideologies in Syria that would place their lives at risk. The male claimant, in addition to earlier statements referenced as to why he and the female claimant are not baptized; stated that the main issue as to why the claimants are not baptized is that the claimants were living with his sister in London, Ontario and that they were not able to follow the lessons of the faith at his sister's house and that the groups are small and scattered in many places.

Even if it is remotely true that the claimants could not practice their alleged adopted faith at the male claimant's sister's home in London, Ontario, that does not mean, in the panel's view, that the claimants could not have practiced fully their Jehovah's Witness faith elsewhere with a view of preparing themselves to be baptized at a later date. The panel makes another negative credibility finding which severely negatively impacts the claimants' identity as Jehovah's Witnesses as so alleged.

Furthermore, the panel asked the claimant whether he knows what Jehovah's Witnesses believe about blood transfusions. The male claimant states that the bible says don't eat meat with blood and "that's why we don't take blood transfusions." The claimant went on to say that if blood was required to save his life that he would not accept it as "we have been ordered by Jehovah." The panel has had an opportunity to review exhibit C-5 provided by the claimants. The said exhibit is referred to as the "Advance Medical Directive". While the said exhibit was presented to show the claimants adhere to the directive or practices of Jehovah's Witnesses, the panel has no indication that the directive were issued by the Jehovah's Witnesses elders or from the Jehovah's Witness hierarchy, particularly as the male claimant stated he does not have a blood card, which would state similar information that is provided in the medical directive, as the claimants are not baptized. The panel gives little weight to the documents as so presented.

The panel notes that the claimants' children are currently living in Syria in a rented residence on their own and allegedly are aware of the claimants' involvement in the Jehovah's Witness faith since XXXXX 2011. It does not appear credible to the panel that the children would just become aware of their parents Jehovah's Witness involvement just nine months ago given their apparent communication with their children and even due to their alleged underground meetings in Syria prior to leaving for Canada. The panel makes a negative credibility find as a consequence.

The claimants were asked who they fear. The male claimant indicated that he fears the security forces and his family in Syria as the security forces and the family knows the claimants have converted to the Jehovah's Witness faith and that the children are being "pressured". If the claimants' children were pressured as alleged by security forces and family, it would be expected that the children would have corroborated such evidence. This is not the case and the panel gives little weight to this portion of the claimants' evidence in this regard.

The male claimant's sister in London, Ontario allegedly is aware of the claimants' interest in the Jehovah's Witness faith, which she apparently does not support. Given the male claimant's sister's knowledge, it is likely that family members in Syria would be apprised of such developments and the continued interest in the Jehovah's Witnesses in Canada. The claimants' children continue to reside in Syria to this day without any known persecutory problems from the security forces or the claimants' family, which would be likely given the conditions in Syria today. The panel makes another negative credibility finding.

Furthermore, the panel notes that the male claimant worked as a XXXXX in XXXXX, Syria from XXXXX 2003 until XXXXX 2009. If the male claimant was visited at his home and questioned at a police station or office in XXXXX 2009 by police due to his alleged meetings with Jehovah's Witnesses in Syria, it is not likely that he would have been able to continue working until XXXXX 2009 when the claimants were scheduled to leave Syria and that the authorities would have allowed them to leave the country. The panel has little or no evidence that the male claimant even encountered difficulties at his place of work, that being with the Ministry of XXXXX in XXXXX due to the claimants' alleged meetings since approximately XXXXX 2009 and had difficulties leaving the country. The panel makes a negative credibility finding.

In this case, the claimants have attempted to provide corroborating evidence to support their cases with a view of obtaining a positive determination. The panel does recognize that corroborating evidence is not always required to substantiate a credible claim to refugee protection. However, when the documents do not satisfactorily corroborate the claim, the panel is left with little evidence regarding the genuineness of the claim and that there is a mere possibility of serious harm that would come to the claimants if required to return to Syria.

On the issue of corroborating evidence, the panel wishes to note the following Federal Court case in Bhagat,5 which states the following: Corroborating evidence is not always necessary to establish the applicant's subjective fear. The Board, however, determined that in the particular circumstances of this case, corroborating evidence of persecution was expected. An absence of corroborating evidence, then, permitted it to make a negative inference against credibility of the applicant. The respondent relies on Sheik v. Canada (M.E.I.) (C.A.), [1990] 3 F.C. 238, at page 244, for its argument that the Board did not err in law when making that conclusion: The concept of "credible evidence" is not, of course, the same as that of the credibility of the applicant, but it is obvious that where the only evidence before a tribunal linking the applicant to his claim is that of the applicant himself (in addition, perhaps, to "country reports" from which nothing about the applicant's claim can be directly deduced), a tribunal's perception that he is not a credible witness effectively amounts to a finding that there is no credible evidence on which the second-level tribunal could allow his claim. In Adu v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1995] F.C.J. No. 114 (QL), the Federal Court of Appeal found that it is reasonable to expect documentary evidence of the existence of a law and stated: The "presumption" that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.

The panel asked the claimants what would their families and the security forces do if they were required to return to Syria. With respect to their families, the male claimant stated that he would live in utmost isolation and if he were to die no one would participate in his funeral. Although the male claimant's response makes little sense to the panel, if taken at his word, that in of itself does not amount to future persecution. The panel makes a negative credibility finding as a consequence.

With regard to the claimants' fear of the security forces, the male claimant stated that he would be considered a spy and that Jehovah's Witnesses are believed to be Zionists. Even if the security forces were to believe the claimants are or were affiliated somehow with the underground Jehovah's Witnesses as so alleged in the past, in a forward looking analysis, the panel was not provided with sufficiency of evidence to suggest that the claimants would be persecuted upon return at some point in Syria. The panel makes a negative credibility finding as it relates to the well foundedness of their claims as so presented.

In evaluating the evidence in this case, the panel is mindful of the treatment of religious minorities, like Jehovah's Witnesses in Syria, some discriminatory and some persecutory. The following items referred to below provides some qualitative information about the situation in Syria. The government systematically repressed citizens' ability to change their government. The security forces committed arbitrary or unlawful killings, caused politically motivated disappearances, and tortured and physically abused prisoners and detainees with impunity. Security forces arrested and detained individuals under poor conditions without due process. Lengthy pretrial and incommunicado detention remained a serious problem. The judiciary was not independent. There were political prisoners and detainees, and during the year the government sentenced to prison several high-profile members of the human rights and civil society communities. The government violated citizens' privacy rights. The government imposed severe restrictions on civil liberties: freedoms of speech and press, including Internet and academic freedom; freedoms of assembly and of association, including severe restrictions on nongovernmental organizations (NGOs); and freedoms of religion and movement. An atmosphere of corruption pervaded the government. Violence and societal discrimination against women continued, as did sexual exploitation, increasingly of Iraqi refugees, including minors. The government discriminated against minorities, particularly Kurds, and severely restricted workers' rights.6 Item 12.1 of the index states: The constitution provides for freedom of religion; however, the government imposes restrictions on this right. Government policies and the judicial system allow many groups to worship freely, provided that religious rites do not disturb the public order. The government bans Jehovah's Witnesses, and they must conduct their activities without attracting its attention. Citizens have the legal right to sue the government when they believe it has violated their rights. During the reporting period, there were no known lawsuits against the government over specifically religious issues.7 Item 12.3 of the index states: According to the General Counsel, in Syria, "Jehovah's Witnesses have virtually no freedoms" (4 Nov. 2005). They are still subject to a ban and "are repeatedly and continuously called in for investigation" (Office of Public Information of Jehovah's Witnesses 4 Nov. 2005). Some Jehovah's Witnesses have been subjected to harassment and torture and have been imprisoned because of their religious affiliation (ibid.). The most recent arrest of a Jehovah's Witness in Syria was in 2000 (ibid.). Jehovah's Witnesses are prohibited from congregating for worship and their literature is likewise forbidden (ibid.). The General Counsel said that, in 2004, the home of a Jehovah's Witness was raided by police searching for religious literature (ibid.). Jehovah's Witnesses cannot be employed by the government, and, if a government employee were to become a Jehovah's Witness, he or she would be discharged (ibid.). Moreover, according to the General Counsel, records of the names of Jehovah's Witnesses are kept at the borders because they are not allowed to leave the country (ibid.). The above information could not be corroborated by the sources consulted by the Research Directorate.8

The panel also wishes to note the disclosure submitted by counsel as seen in exhibit C-3, which references the serious, egregious acts committed by Syrian officials against certain people in the country. However, given the credibility concerns in the evidence referred to earlier in these reasons and the alleged identity of the claimants as Jehovah's Witnesses, inclusive of the fact that the panel has little or no credible evidence as to the claimants' profile as alleged and that their lives are at risk as a consequence, there is insufficient evidence that would cause this panel to believe these claims as presented.

Therefore, in a forward looking analysis, there is little or no credible evidence the panel has to conclude that the evidence provided by the claimants is trustworthy enough to believe that the claimants' lives are at risk based on what has been alleged. In this particular case, the panel does not know what to believe. Conclusion

Having considered all the evidence and based on the above analysis, the panel finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees as they have not established that there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility that they would be persecuted for a Convention ground or there would be a risk to their lives or they would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should they be required to return to Syria. On substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture should the claimants return to Syria. The panel rejects these claims pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. (signed) "K. Dickenson" K.
